chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
title: Intonation, Blanton, and a good ear
summary: Crouch compares his intonation to Jimmy Blanton's; Stewart credits focused practice, a good ear and strong fingers.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Now, you -- so that you developed this -- yeah, good. Good. Good. Now, how did you come -- like I've known you since you have very good -- see like, one of the things obviously that stands out about somebody like Jimmy Blanton, for instance, is that he played with incredible intonation.

And you play with rather incredible intonation as well. Now, I've noticed that in listening to a lot of the bassists from the '30s, that they didn't always tend necessarily to hit the notes, at least as what the records tell. Their intonation wasn't necessarily always as good as one might have wished.
Now, was there a way -- did you achieve your intonation control by having a good ear or by specifically focusing on that when you were practicing?
Well, I was focusing on that while I

was practicing, and at the same time I was blessed, you might say, with a very good ear, you know. I could hear very well. And that was such a big help. And my approach to the bass, somehow I had quite a bit of strength, you know, in my hands, in my fingers, where when I was plucking, that I could really bring those notes out, you know. That was -- very thankful for that, you know.
